timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.name: Edit
schema.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: EnterWorktree
tools.description:
Use this tool ONLY when explicitly instructed to work in a worktree — either by the user directly, or by project instructions (CLAUDE.md / memory). This tool creates an isolated git worktree and switches the current session into it.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly says "worktree" (e.g., "start a worktree", "work in a worktree", "create a worktree", "use a worktree")
- CLAUDE.md or memory instructions direct you to work in a worktree for the current task

## When NOT to Use

- The user asks to create a branch, switch branches, or work on a different branch — use git commands instead
- The user asks to fix a bug or work on a feature — use normal git workflow unless worktrees are explicitly requested by the user or project instructions
- Never use this tool unless "worktree" is explicitly mentioned by the user or in CLAUDE.md / memory instructions

## Requirements

- Must be in a git repository, OR have WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks configured in settings.json
- Must not already be in a worktree session when creating a new worktree (`name`); switching into another existing worktree via `path` is allowed

## Behavior

- In a git repository: creates a new git worktree inside `.claude/worktrees/` on a new branch. The base ref is governed by the `worktree.baseRef` setting: `fresh` (default) branches from origin/<default-branch>; `head` branches from your current local HEAD
- Outside a git repository: delegates to WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks for VCS-agnostic isolation
- Switches the session's working directory to the new worktree
- Use ExitWorktree to leave the worktree mid-session (keep or remove). On session exit, if still in the worktree, the user will be prompted to keep or remove it

## Entering an existing worktree

Pass `path` instead of `name` to switch the session into a worktree that already exists (e.g., one you just created with `git worktree add`). On first entry from the launch directory, the path must appear in `git worktree list` for the repository that owns it — the current repository or, in a multi-repo workspace, a repository nested inside it; paths registered by neither are rejected. ExitWorktree will not remove a worktree entered this way; use `action: "keep"` to return to the original directory.

Switching with `path` also works when the session is already in a worktree (the previous worktree is left on disk, untouched, and only the new one is tracked for exit-time cleanup), and from agents whose working directory was pinned at launch (subagent isolation or explicit cwd). In both cases the target must be a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` of the same repository, and from a pinned agent the switch only affects this agent, not the parent session. After a further switch, previously-visited worktrees are no longer writable — re-issue EnterWorktree with `path` to return to one.

## Parameters

- `name` (optional): A name for a new worktree. If neither `name` nor `path` is provided, a random name is generated.
- `path` (optional): Path to an existing worktree to enter instead of creating one — of the current repository, or (on first entry from the launch directory) of a repository nested inside it. Mutually exclusive with `name`.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. ## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. Authenticated searches always add alexandria to the sources, so sources: ["web"] also returns providers; domainTools: false turns off website-matched tools only. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. firecrawl_search_feedback records a quality rating for a prior firecrawl_search by its id. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If
  background control still cannot work, report that limitation instead of
  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.
- The normal local flow attaches to the running Chrome/Chromium CDP endpoint. No browser ids or local profile selection.

  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome

  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.

 "identityCheck": "Title in the text matches the filename ('Mechanisms, injury patterns, and kinematic features of hamstring strain injuries in football (soccer): a systematic review and meta-analysis of video-analysis studies') and the printed article DOI is 10.3389/fpubh.2026.1846524.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Performance", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 7 match video-analysis studies covering 342 hamstring strain injuries in 11-a-side football, mostly from professional male players (six male studies, one female study). The authors report higher relative reporting of non-contact vs indirect-contact injuries (OR 2.51, 95% CI 1.31 to 4.82) and of sprint-type vs mixed-type injuries (OR 2.01, 95% CI 1.04 to 3.87). Sprint vs stretch, offensive vs defensive, and first vs second half showed no clear difference.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only seven small studies were pooled, with heterogeneity of I2 67% to 71% for the two significant comparisons and 84% for sprint vs stretch. Video studies have no exposure-time denominators, so the results describe reported event patterns, not injury risk.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the odds ratios as proof of injury risk factors or as evidence that a specific training or prevention strategy works, but the authors say video data cannot show that any training strategy prevents hamstring injury.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2026,
   "citation": "Xia J, He J, Yao J, Zhu Y, Mao L, Zhu X. Mechanisms, injury patterns, and kinematic features of hamstring strain injuries in football (soccer): a systematic review and meta-analysis of video-analysis studies. Front Public Health. 2026;14:1846524.",
   "doi": "10.3389/fpubh.2026.1846524",
   "abstract": "This meta-analysis pooled seven football match video-analysis studies of 342 hamstring strain injuries. Non-contact and sprint-type injuries were reported more often than indirect-contact and mixed-type injuries. Offensive vs defensive phase, first vs second half, and sprint vs stretch mechanisms showed no clear difference.",
   "tldr": "Match video studies of football hamstring injuries most often describe non-contact, sprint-type events. The evidence is small and inconsistent, and it cannot show which training or prevention strategies would reduce these injuries.",
   "methods": "Seven databases were searched to 12 February 2026, and the protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261335634) after the preliminary search but before screening. Eligible studies used video analysis of real-match hamstring injuries in 11-a-side football, and five prespecified odds ratios were pooled with DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models restricted to male samples. Single-arm proportions were pooled with a generalized linear mixed model, and quality was rated with JBI, STROBE-SIIS and QA-SIVAS.",
   "findings": "Non-contact vs indirect contact gave OR 2.51 (95% CI 1.31 to 4.82, p = 0.006, I2 = 71%), and sprint-type vs mixed-type gave OR 2.01 (95% CI 1.04 to 3.87, p = 0.037, I2 = 67%). Sprint vs stretch (OR 1.64, 95% CI 0.74 to 3.61), offensive vs defensive (OR 0.99) and first vs second half (OR 1.13) showed no clear difference. Kinematic and sex comparisons were exploratory, and no sex difference survived multiple-comparison correction.",
   "limitations": "Only seven studies and 342 cases were included, with mechanism definitions and video standards that differ across studies. Five of the seven were rated high risk of bias by JBI, and the two significant results rest on nominal p values with wide confidence intervals. The female evidence comes from one study, and the reference list numbering for two studies is inconsistent between text and Table 3 (no effect on the reported results).",
   "practicalImplications": "Staff can use the pattern of non-contact, sprint-type events to frame questions about high-speed running exposure, eccentric load tolerance and single-leg support in monitoring and prevention work. The paper does not show that any specific exercise, dose or load reduces hamstring injury.",
   "athleteDev": "For performance staff, the pattern points to high-speed running and late-swing eccentric loading as the setting to examine when reviewing sprint exposure and eccentric tolerance. The review gives no dose, load or exercise prescription and reports no training effect on hamstring injury.",
   "rtp": "This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It describes how hamstring injuries happen in match play and reports no recovery, readiness, re-injury or return-timing data, so use it only as background on injury mechanism."
 }
}

1	2026, VOL. 58, NO. 1, 2652116
2	https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2026.2652116
3	
4	
5	RESEARCH ARTICLE
6	
7	Intervention components, training dose, and adherence in exercise-
8	based prevention of hamstring strain injury in football: a systematic
9	review and meta-analysis
10	Jinfa Gua,b*           , Yan Lic*          , Yinhao Wangd                 and Yu Zhanga
11	a
12	 Qilu Medical University, Zibo, China; bExercise & Sports Science Programme, School of Health Sciences, Universiti Sains
13	Malaysia, Kubang Kerian, Kelantan, Malaysia; cDepartment of Pharmacy, Ezhou Central Hospital, Ezhou, Hubei, China;
14	d
15	  Department of Physical Education, Guilin University of Technology, Guilin, China
16	
17	
18	    ABSTRACT                                                                                                                    ARTICLE HISTORY
19	    Objective: To quantify associations between exercise-based prevention programmes                                            Received 9 January 2026
20	    and hamstring strain injury (HSI) risk in football participants, and whether training dose                                  Accepted 24 March 2026
21	    and adherence modify effects.                                                                                               KEYWORDS
22	    Methods: Six databases were searched to 1 October 2025. Randomised and                                                      Hamstring injury; injury
23	    cluster-randomised trials comparing HSI prevention programmes with usual practice or                                        prevention; adherence;
24	    warm-up in football participants were included. Random-effects meta-analysis pooled                                         football; meta-analysis
25	    risk ratios (RRs); subgroup analyses and meta-regression assessed effect modification.
26	    Results: Fifteen trials (n = 7,465) were analysed. Programmes reduced HSI risk (RR =
27	    0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.71), with I²=57% and a prediction interval crossing the null (0.18–
28	    1.40). Based on a control event rate of 7.8%, absolute risk reduction was 3.8% (38 fewer
29	    HSIs per 1000 participants; 95% CI 23–50 fewer). Effects were stronger for shorter
30	    interventions (1–6 months; RR = 0.43) than longer interventions (7–10 months; RR =
31	    0.77; P for interaction=0.04), and for elite/semi-professional players (RR = 0.38) than
32	    amateur players (RR = 0.77; P for interaction = 0.02). Training frequency and weekly
33	    volume did not modify effects, whereas adherence did. High adherence (≥75%) was
34	    associated with lower HSI risk (RR = 0.36, 95% CI 0.28–0.48), whereas low adherence
35	    (<75%) showed no clear benefit (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23; P for interaction <0.00001).
36	    Each 10% increase in adherence corresponded to an RR multiplier of 0.83 (approximately
37	    17% lower RR). Certainty of evidence was low.
38	    Conclusion: Exercise-based programmes reduce HSI risk in football when implementation
39	    supports sustained adherence. Effects may be stronger in shorter interventions and
40	    elite populations, but evidence remains insufficient to differentiate programme types or
41	    components.
42	
43	
44	
45	
46	1. Introduction
47	Hamstring strain injury (HSI) is among the most frequent non-contact muscle injuries in football (associ-
48	ation football; soccer) and typically occurs during sprinting, rapid deceleration, and cutting actions [1,2].
49	HSIs represent a major burden in professional football, accounting for substantial absence days (approx-
50	imately 25% of all injury-related absences) and requiring meaningful time loss for return to play (mean
51	9 days) [3]. Incidence estimates vary across cohorts and settings, with reports ranging from 1.06 to 5.87
52	injuries per 1000 h of exposure [4]. Surveillance in elite European teams indicates that a greater propor-
53	tion of HSIs occur during match play than training, underscoring their close association with high-intensity
54	game demands [5]. Beyond availability, HSIs impose substantial competitive and economic costs in elite
55	football [3,6].
56	
57	CONTACT Yu Zhang         1163572919@qq.com          Qilu Medical University, Zibo, China.
58	*These authors contributed equally to this work.
59	    Supplemental data for this article can be accessed online at https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2026.2652116.
60	© 2026 The Author(s). Published by Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group
61	This is an Open Access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/
62	by-nc/4.0/), which permits unrestricted non-commercial use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited. The terms
63	on which this article has been published allow the posting of the Accepted Manuscript in a repository by the author(s) or with their consent.
64	 2     J. GU ET AL.
65	
66	
67	    Recurrence rates of 12–16% within the first year further compound the burden [7,8]. Collectively,
68	these factors position HSI prevention as a practical priority in applied football settings [9–11].
69	    Additionally, exercise-based prevention programmes represent the primary approach to HSI preven-
70	tion. Preventive strategies evaluated in football include eccentric strengthening protocols such as the
71	Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE), structured warm-up programmes such as FIFA 11/11+, and multicom-
72	ponent programmes incorporating core stability and balance training [12,13]. Meta-analytic evidence
73	generally supports risk reduction when the NHE is included within prevention programmes, with pooled
74	estimates indicating that hamstring injury rates may be reduced by approximately half [14]. Evidence
75	syntheses also suggest that eccentric resistance training and FIFA 11+ can decrease HSI occurrence in
76	athletic populations, with some meta-analyses reporting reductions of up to 50% [15,16]. However, trans-
77	lation into football practice is complicated by variability in programme content (isolated eccentric train-
78	ing vs multicomponent programmes), prescription (frequency, volume, progression), delivery (integration
79	into routine practice, supervision), and adherence [17–19].
80	    Moreover, HSIs are commonly linked to repeated eccentric contractions and high muscular tension
81	demands, supporting eccentric strengthening as a logical preventive target [19,20]. In parallel, modifiable
82	factors such as strength and muscle architecture have been highlighted as key targets for
83	prevention-oriented programming [21,22]. Multicomponent programmes may additionally influence HSI
84	risk by improving movement control and load management during high-speed running and directional
85	changes [23]. Therefore, the present study examines whether preventive effects differ by programme
86	type, constituent elements, training dose, and adherence [9].
87	    Despite extensive research, key implementation limitations remain. High-level teams may not adopt
88	HSI prevention protocols consistently, and delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is commonly cited as
89	a perceived barrier to the uptake of eccentric-focused exercises such as the NHE, although direct empir-
90	ical evidence linking DOMS to reduced adherence in trials remains limited [17,24,25]. Furthermore, adher-
91	ence appears to meaningfully influence effectiveness, yet has not been consistently quantified across
92	trials and reviews [14,15,18]. For example, fewer than 15% of teams have been reported to complete the
93	recommended FIFA 11+ volume, which may compromise real-world effectiveness [26]. Additionally, meth-
94	odological critiques have questioned the certainty of some large effect estimates, suggesting that rec-
95	ommendations may be conditional on study design and analytic choices [27]. These issues collectively
96	reinforce the need for synthesis approaches that explicitly account for programme modality and imple-
97	mentation factors, particularly adherence and dose.
98	    Accordingly, the primary objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to quantify the
99	association between exercise-based hamstring injury prevention programmes and hamstring strain injury
100	(HSI) risk in football participants. Secondary objectives were to assess whether prescribed training dose,
101	adherence, and playing level modify programme effects. Exploratory analyses compared intervention
102	types, specific programme components, and programme complexity, and meta-regression quantified the
103	adherence–effect association.
104	
105	
106	2. Methods
107	2.1. Methodology and literature search strategy
108	This meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251246295) and reported in accordance with
109	the PRISMA 2020 guidelines [28]. A completed PRISMA 2020 checklist is provided as Supplementary
110	File 1. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, the
111	Cochrane Library, EBSCOhost-SportDiscus, and EMBASE from database inception. The final search was
112	completed on 1 October 2025. Searches were limited to full-text, peer-reviewed journal articles pub-
113	lished in English. The search strategy was developed based on the PICOS (Population, Intervention,
114	Comparison, Outcomes, Study design) framework [29], and the search strategies are provided in the
115	(Supplementary Material Table S1), with any remaining database-specific strategies available on
116	request. Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles were hand-searched to identify further eligible
117	studies.
118	                                                                                     Annals of Medicine     3
119	
120	
121	2.2. Inclusion and exclusion criteria
122	Randomised controlled or cluster-randomised trials in football participants and other football-related
123	cohorts were eligible if they compared an exercise-based hamstring injury prevention programme with
124	usual practice or a standard warm-up, and reported HSI events as event counts. The referee trial was
125	included; its influence was assessed in sensitivity analyses. HSI was extracted as defined in each trial and
126	analysed as total HSI events (including first-time and recurrent injuries when reported). Usual practice/
127	standard warm-up referred to the team’s routine training and warm-up activities without an additional
128	structured HSI prevention programme. Studies enrolling mixed populations were eligible if football-specific
129	HSI data could be extracted separately.
130	    Furthermore, studies were excluded if they used non-randomised designs, evaluated rehabilitation or
131	post-surgical interventions, did not report HSI-specific outcomes (or did not allow extraction of
132	football-specific HSI data), involved non-football cohorts without separable data, or were not available as
133	full-text articles. Reviews, case reports, and animal studies were also excluded.
134	
135	
136	2.3. Data extraction
137	Two reviewers independently extracted data using a prespecified form and entered them into a stan-
138	dardised spreadsheet. Data extraction covered study and participant characteristics (country, sex, age,
139	and playing level) and intervention characteristics (type, duration, session frequency, session duration,
140	and adherence). The population variable distinguished football participants from other football-related
141	cohorts, such as referees. Intervention content was further coded according to predefined components
142	(strength, balance, plyometrics, agility/speed, and flexibility) and by whether the programme incorpo-
143	rated eccentric hamstring training. Then, the programme complexity was classified as single- or
144	dual-component versus multicomponent (≥3 components). Discrepancies were resolved by consensus
145	and, when necessary, by adjudication from a third author. The complete extracted dataset is provided in
146	the online supplementary material.
147	
148	
149	2.4. Quality assessment
150	Methodological quality was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool [30], covering five
151	domains: the randomisation process, departures from intended interventions, missing outcome data, out-
152	come measurement, and selection of the reported result. Assessments were completed independently by
153	two reviewers. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus and, when necessary, by adjudication from a
154	third author. RoB 2 was applied at the outcome level (HSI) for each trial. Overall risk of bias for each
155	study was determined according to the RoB 2 algorithm (low risk, some concerns, or high risk).
156	
157	
158	2.5. Certainty of the evidence
159	The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment,
160	Development and Evaluation) framework [31], considering risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, impre-
161	cision, and publication bias, with findings rated as high, moderate, low, or very low certainty.
162	
163	
164	2.6. Data analysis
165	Effect sizes were expressed as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and analysed on the
166	log scale. For each study, log RRs and corresponding standard errors were obtained or derived from the
167	reported data in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [32].
168	For studies reporting injury incidence rates, event counts were extracted when available to enable con-
169	sistent RR estimation. For cluster-randomised trials, we used effect estimates as reported in the original
170	publications when available; otherwise, risk ratios were derived from the reported event counts at the
171	study level. For studies with zero events in one arm, a continuity correction of 0.5 was applied to enable
172	 4     J. GU ET AL.
173	
174	
175	estimation of risk ratios. Pooled estimates were obtained using inverse-variance weighting under a
176	random-effects model [33]. Statistical heterogeneity was evaluated using Cochran’s Q and quantified with
177	the I2 statistic. Subsequently, between-study variance (τ2) was estimated, and prediction intervals for the
178	pooled effect were calculated.
179	    Prespecified subgroup analyses examined whether effects differed by training dose (intervention period,
180	session frequency, session duration, and weekly training volume), adherence (low <75% vs high ≥75%),
181	and playing level. High adherence was defined as completing ≥75% of prescribed training sessions.
182	Adherence information was extracted from trial reports and standardised as the percentage of prescribed
183	sessions completed (relative to the prescribed number) for analysis at the study level in our subgroup and
184	meta-regression analyses. Exploratory subgroup analyses assessed intervention type, specific programme
185	components (strength, balance, plyometrics, agility/speed, flexibility, and eccentric hamstring training), and
186	programme complexity. Programme complexity was defined a priori as single- or dual-component versus
187	multicomponent, with multicomponent programmes comprising three or more components. Studies were
188	excluded from adherence-based analyses when adherence data were unavailable.
189	    Random-effects meta-regression was conducted to examine the association between adherence (%)
190	and intervention effects on the logRR scale. Sensitivity analyses assessed robustness using leave-one-out
191	procedures and re-estimation under a fixed-effect model. In addition, the primary meta-analysis was
192	repeated excluding studies judged to be at high risk of bias overall. Publication bias was assessed visu-
193	ally using funnel plots and statistically using Egger’s regression and Begg’s rank correlation tests when
194	at least ten studies were available [34,35]. When asymmetry was suggested, the trim-and-fill method was
195	applied.
196	    All analyses were conducted in R (v4.4.3) in RStudio, primarily using the meta and metafor packages.
197	
198	
199	3. Results
200	3.1. Literature search results
201	A systematic search of six databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and
202	EBSCOhost-SportDiscus) identified 1,481 records. After removing 449 duplicates, 1,032 records were
203	screened at the title and abstract level, of which 968 were excluded (968/1,032; 93.8%). Sixty-four full-text
204	reports were sought; seven could not be obtained (7/64; 10.9%), leaving 57 for eligibility assessment. At
205	full-text review, 46 reports were excluded (46/57; 80.7%) due to no injury outcomes reported (19/46;
206	41.3%), insufficient data for analysis (17/46; 37.0%), or ineligible study design (10/46; 21.7%). Citation
207	searching identified four additional records, all of which met the eligibility criteria (4/4; 100%). In total,
208	15 studies were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis (Figure 1).
209	
210	
211	3.2. Characteristics of included studies
212	Fifteen trials were included (Table 1), enrolling football participants aged 13–45 years across ten coun-
213	tries [10,36–50]. Eleven studies included male-only cohorts, and four included female-only cohorts.
214	Competitive level ranged from high school and amateur to semi-professional, professional, collegiate,
215	and elite teams; one study enrolled amateur referees, whereas the remaining trials enrolled football
216	players.
217	    Furthermore, the interventions were exercise-based injury prevention protocols integrated into routine
218	training. Programmes evaluated FIFA 11+ (n = 4), the NHE alone (n = 4), NHE with additional components
219	(n = 3), and single trials of balance-board training, plyometric bounding, flywheel training, and a multi-
220	modal programme. Prescribed training dose ranged from 1.5 to 3.5 sessions/week (median 2) over
221	7–43 weeks (median 21). Session duration was reported in 11/15 trials (4–20 min), most commonly around
222	15 min. Adherence was reported in 14/15 trials, ranging from 21% to 100% (median 84%).
223	    Across interventions (Table 2), strength elements were present in 14/15 trials and eccentric hamstring
224	training in 12/15. The balance, plyometrics, and flexibility components each appeared in 6/15 trials,
225	whereas the agility/speed components appeared in 5/15. By intervention type, FIFA 11+ accounted for
226	4/15 trials, NHE-focused protocols (including combinations) for 7/15, and other interventions for 4/15.
227	                                                                                             Annals of Medicine        5
228	
229	
230	
231	
232	Figure 1. PRISMA flow diagram illustrating the study selection process for the systematic review and meta-analysis.
233	
234	Most interventions were single- or dual-component (10/15), with multicomponent programmes (≥3 com-
235	ponents) comprising 5/15.
236	
237	
238	3.3. Risk of bias assessment
239	Methodological quality for the 15 included studies was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool (Figure 2).
240	Overall, one study (1/15) was judged to be at low risk of bias, twelve studies (12/15) raised some concerns,
241	and two studies (2/15) were at high risk of bias. Domain-level assessment indicated that deviations from
242	the intended interventions (D2) were the most common issue, raising some concerns in 14 out of 15 stud-
243	ies (14/15). Missing outcome data (D3) raised concerns in three studies (3/15), and selection of the reported
244	result (D5) raised concerns in two studies (2/15). In contrast, the randomisation process (D1) demonstrated
245	high methodological quality across most studies (14/15 at low risk), and measurement of the outcome (D4)
246	was at low risk in most studies (13/15). These limitations, largely related to deviations from intended inter-
247	ventions, may have attenuated the estimated intervention effects.
248	
249	
250	3.4. Evaluation of meta-analysis results
251	3.4.1. Overall effect test
252	A meta-analysis of 15 randomised and cluster-randomised trials (n = 7,465) showed that exercise-based
253	prevention programmes significantly reduced the risk of HSI in football participants (RR = 0.51, 95% CI
254	0.36–0.71; p < 0.0001), corresponding to an approximately 49% relative risk reduction (1 − RR).
255	Between-study heterogeneity was moderate (I2 = 57%, τ2 = 0.20). The 95% prediction interval ranged
256	from 0.18 to 1.40. It crossed the line of no effect (RR = 1), indicating that the magnitude of benefit might
257	vary across implementation contexts. 14 of the 15 studies had point estimates favouring the intervention
258	(RR < 1), supporting consistency in the direction of the overall effect (Figure 3).

Intervention components, training dose, and adherence in exercise-
based prevention of hamstring strain injury in football: a systematic
review and meta-analysis
Jinfa Gua,b*           , Yan Lic*          , Yinhao Wangd                 and Yu Zhanga

    ABSTRACT                                                                                                                    ARTICLE HISTORY
    Objective: To quantify associations between exercise-based prevention programmes                                            Received 9 January 2026
    and hamstring strain injury (HSI) risk in football participants, and whether training dose                                  Accepted 24 March 2026
    and adherence modify effects.                                                                                               KEYWORDS
    Methods: Six databases were searched to 1 October 2025. Randomised and                                                      Hamstring injury; injury
    cluster-randomised trials comparing HSI prevention programmes with usual practice or                                        prevention; adherence;
    warm-up in football participants were included. Random-effects meta-analysis pooled                                         football; meta-analysis
    risk ratios (RRs); subgroup analyses and meta-regression assessed effect modification.
    Results: Fifteen trials (n = 7,465) were analysed. Programmes reduced HSI risk (RR =
    0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.71), with I²=57% and a prediction interval crossing the null (0.18–
    1.40). Based on a control event rate of 7.8%, absolute risk reduction was 3.8% (38 fewer
    HSIs per 1000 participants; 95% CI 23–50 fewer). Effects were stronger for shorter
    interventions (1–6 months; RR = 0.43) than longer interventions (7–10 months; RR =
    0.77; P for interaction=0.04), and for elite/semi-professional players (RR = 0.38) than
    amateur players (RR = 0.77; P for interaction = 0.02). Training frequency and weekly
    volume did not modify effects, whereas adherence did. High adherence (≥75%) was
    associated with lower HSI risk (RR = 0.36, 95% CI 0.28–0.48), whereas low adherence
    (<75%) showed no clear benefit (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23; P for interaction <0.00001).
    Each 10% increase in adherence corresponded to an RR multiplier of 0.83 (approximately
    17% lower RR). Certainty of evidence was low.
    Conclusion: Exercise-based programmes reduce HSI risk in football when implementation
    supports sustained adherence. Effects may be stronger in shorter interventions and
    elite populations, but evidence remains insufficient to differentiate programme types or
    components.




1. Introduction
Hamstring strain injury (HSI) is among the most frequent non-contact muscle injuries in football (associ-
ation football; soccer) and typically occurs during sprinting, rapid deceleration, and cutting actions [1,2].
HSIs represent a major burden in professional football, accounting for substantial absence days (approx-
imately 25% of all injury-related absences) and requiring meaningful time loss for return to play (mean
9 days) [3]. Incidence estimates vary across cohorts and settings, with reports ranging from 1.06 to 5.87
injuries per 1000 h of exposure [4]. Surveillance in elite European teams indicates that a greater propor-
tion of HSIs occur during match play than training, underscoring their close association with high-intensity
game demands [5]. Beyond availability, HSIs impose substantial competitive and economic costs in elite
football [3,6].

    Recurrence rates of 12–16% within the first year further compound the burden [7,8]. Collectively,
these factors position HSI prevention as a practical priority in applied football settings [9–11].
    Additionally, exercise-based prevention programmes represent the primary approach to HSI preven-
tion. Preventive strategies evaluated in football include eccentric strengthening protocols such as the
Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE), structured warm-up programmes such as FIFA 11/11+, and multicom-
ponent programmes incorporating core stability and balance training [12,13]. Meta-analytic evidence
generally supports risk reduction when the NHE is included within prevention programmes, with pooled
estimates indicating that hamstring injury rates may be reduced by approximately half [14]. Evidence
syntheses also suggest that eccentric resistance training and FIFA 11+ can decrease HSI occurrence in
athletic populations, with some meta-analyses reporting reductions of up to 50% [15,16]. However, trans-
lation into football practice is complicated by variability in programme content (isolated eccentric train-
ing vs multicomponent programmes), prescription (frequency, volume, progression), delivery (integration
into routine practice, supervision), and adherence [17–19].
    Moreover, HSIs are commonly linked to repeated eccentric contractions and high muscular tension
demands, supporting eccentric strengthening as a logical preventive target [19,20]. In parallel, modifiable
factors such as strength and muscle architecture have been highlighted as key targets for
prevention-oriented programming [21,22]. Multicomponent programmes may additionally influence HSI
risk by improving movement control and load management during high-speed running and directional
changes [23]. Therefore, the present study examines whether preventive effects differ by programme
type, constituent elements, training dose, and adherence [9].
    Despite extensive research, key implementation limitations remain. High-level teams may not adopt
HSI prevention protocols consistently, and delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is commonly cited as
a perceived barrier to the uptake of eccentric-focused exercises such as the NHE, although direct empir-
ical evidence linking DOMS to reduced adherence in trials remains limited [17,24,25]. Furthermore, adher-
ence appears to meaningfully influence effectiveness, yet has not been consistently quantified across
trials and reviews [14,15,18]. For example, fewer than 15% of teams have been reported to complete the
recommended FIFA 11+ volume, which may compromise real-world effectiveness [26]. Additionally, meth-
odological critiques have questioned the certainty of some large effect estimates, suggesting that rec-
ommendations may be conditional on study design and analytic choices [27]. These issues collectively
reinforce the need for synthesis approaches that explicitly account for programme modality and imple-
mentation factors, particularly adherence and dose.
    Accordingly, the primary objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to quantify the
association between exercise-based hamstring injury prevention programmes and hamstring strain injury
(HSI) risk in football participants. Secondary objectives were to assess whether prescribed training dose,
adherence, and playing level modify programme effects. Exploratory analyses compared intervention
types, specific programme components, and programme complexity, and meta-regression quantified the
adherence–effect association.


2. Methods
2.1. Methodology and literature search strategy
This meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251246295) and reported in accordance with
the PRISMA 2020 guidelines [28]. A completed PRISMA 2020 checklist is provided as Supplementary
File 1. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, the
Cochrane Library, EBSCOhost-SportDiscus, and EMBASE from database inception. The final search was
completed on 1 October 2025. Searches were limited to full-text, peer-reviewed journal articles pub-
lished in English. The search strategy was developed based on the PICOS (Population, Intervention,
Comparison, Outcomes, Study design) framework [29], and the search strategies are provided in the
(Supplementary Material Table S1), with any remaining database-specific strategies available on
request. Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles were hand-searched to identify further eligible
studies.
                                                                                     Annals of Medicine     3


2.2. Inclusion and exclusion criteria
Randomised controlled or cluster-randomised trials in football participants and other football-related
cohorts were eligible if they compared an exercise-based hamstring injury prevention programme with
usual practice or a standard warm-up, and reported HSI events as event counts. The referee trial was
included; its influence was assessed in sensitivity analyses. HSI was extracted as defined in each trial and
analysed as total HSI events (including first-time and recurrent injuries when reported). Usual practice/
standard warm-up referred to the team’s routine training and warm-up activities without an additional
structured HSI prevention programme. Studies enrolling mixed populations were eligible if football-specific
HSI data could be extracted separately.
    Furthermore, studies were excluded if they used non-randomised designs, evaluated rehabilitation or
post-surgical interventions, did not report HSI-specific outcomes (or did not allow extraction of
football-specific HSI data), involved non-football cohorts without separable data, or were not available as
full-text articles. Reviews, case reports, and animal studies were also excluded.


2.3. Data extraction
Two reviewers independently extracted data using a prespecified form and entered them into a stan-
dardised spreadsheet. Data extraction covered study and participant characteristics (country, sex, age,
and playing level) and intervention characteristics (type, duration, session frequency, session duration,
and adherence). The population variable distinguished football participants from other football-related
cohorts, such as referees. Intervention content was further coded according to predefined components
(strength, balance, plyometrics, agility/speed, and flexibility) and by whether the programme incorpo-
rated eccentric hamstring training. Then, the programme complexity was classified as single- or
dual-component versus multicomponent (≥3 components). Discrepancies were resolved by consensus
and, when necessary, by adjudication from a third author. The complete extracted dataset is provided in
the online supplementary material.


2.4. Quality assessment
Methodological quality was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool [30], covering five
domains: the randomisation process, departures from intended interventions, missing outcome data, out-
come measurement, and selection of the reported result. Assessments were completed independently by
two reviewers. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus and, when necessary, by adjudication from a
third author. RoB 2 was applied at the outcome level (HSI) for each trial. Overall risk of bias for each
study was determined according to the RoB 2 algorithm (low risk, some concerns, or high risk).


2.5. Certainty of the evidence
The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment,
Development and Evaluation) framework [31], considering risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, impre-
cision, and publication bias, with findings rated as high, moderate, low, or very low certainty.


2.6. Data analysis
Effect sizes were expressed as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and analysed on the
log scale. For each study, log RRs and corresponding standard errors were obtained or derived from the
reported data in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [32].
For studies reporting injury incidence rates, event counts were extracted when available to enable con-
sistent RR estimation. For cluster-randomised trials, we used effect estimates as reported in the original
publications when available; otherwise, risk ratios were derived from the reported event counts at the
study level. For studies with zero events in one arm, a continuity correction of 0.5 was applied to enable
 4     J. GU ET AL.


estimation of risk ratios. Pooled estimates were obtained using inverse-variance weighting under a
random-effects model [33]. Statistical heterogeneity was evaluated using Cochran’s Q and quantified with
the I2 statistic. Subsequently, between-study variance (τ2) was estimated, and prediction intervals for the
pooled effect were calculated.
    Prespecified subgroup analyses examined whether effects differed by training dose (intervention period,
session frequency, session duration, and weekly training volume), adherence (low <75% vs high ≥75%),
and playing level. High adherence was defined as completing ≥75% of prescribed training sessions.
Adherence information was extracted from trial reports and standardised as the percentage of prescribed
sessions completed (relative to the prescribed number) for analysis at the study level in our subgroup and
meta-regression analyses. Exploratory subgroup analyses assessed intervention type, specific programme
components (strength, balance, plyometrics, agility/speed, flexibility, and eccentric hamstring training), and
programme complexity. Programme complexity was defined a priori as single- or dual-component versus
multicomponent, with multicomponent programmes comprising three or more components. Studies were
excluded from adherence-based analyses when adherence data were unavailable.
    Random-effects meta-regression was conducted to examine the association between adherence (%)
and intervention effects on the logRR scale. Sensitivity analyses assessed robustness using leave-one-out
procedures and re-estimation under a fixed-effect model. In addition, the primary meta-analysis was
repeated excluding studies judged to be at high risk of bias overall. Publication bias was assessed visu-
ally using funnel plots and statistically using Egger’s regression and Begg’s rank correlation tests when
at least ten studies were available [34,35]. When asymmetry was suggested, the trim-and-fill method was
applied.
    All analyses were conducted in R (v4.4.3) in RStudio, primarily using the meta and metafor packages.


3. Results
3.1. Literature search results
A systematic search of six databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and
EBSCOhost-SportDiscus) identified 1,481 records. After removing 449 duplicates, 1,032 records were
screened at the title and abstract level, of which 968 were excluded (968/1,032; 93.8%). Sixty-four full-text
reports were sought; seven could not be obtained (7/64; 10.9%), leaving 57 for eligibility assessment. At
full-text review, 46 reports were excluded (46/57; 80.7%) due to no injury outcomes reported (19/46;
41.3%), insufficient data for analysis (17/46; 37.0%), or ineligible study design (10/46; 21.7%). Citation
searching identified four additional records, all of which met the eligibility criteria (4/4; 100%). In total,
15 studies were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis (Figure 1).


3.2. Characteristics of included studies
Fifteen trials were included (Table 1), enrolling football participants aged 13–45 years across ten coun-
tries [10,36–50]. Eleven studies included male-only cohorts, and four included female-only cohorts.
Competitive level ranged from high school and amateur to semi-professional, professional, collegiate,
and elite teams; one study enrolled amateur referees, whereas the remaining trials enrolled football
players.
    Furthermore, the interventions were exercise-based injury prevention protocols integrated into routine
training. Programmes evaluated FIFA 11+ (n = 4), the NHE alone (n = 4), NHE with additional components
(n = 3), and single trials of balance-board training, plyometric bounding, flywheel training, and a multi-
modal programme. Prescribed training dose ranged from 1.5 to 3.5 sessions/week (median 2) over
7–43 weeks (median 21). Session duration was reported in 11/15 trials (4–20 min), most commonly around
15 min. Adherence was reported in 14/15 trials, ranging from 21% to 100% (median 84%).
    Across interventions (Table 2), strength elements were present in 14/15 trials and eccentric hamstring
training in 12/15. The balance, plyometrics, and flexibility components each appeared in 6/15 trials,
whereas the agility/speed components appeared in 5/15. By intervention type, FIFA 11+ accounted for
4/15 trials, NHE-focused protocols (including combinations) for 7/15, and other interventions for 4/15.
                                                                                             Annals of Medicine        5




Figure 1. PRISMA flow diagram illustrating the study selection process for the systematic review and meta-analysis.

Most interventions were single- or dual-component (10/15), with multicomponent programmes (≥3 com-
ponents) comprising 5/15.


3.3. Risk of bias assessment
Methodological quality for the 15 included studies was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool (Figure 2).
Overall, one study (1/15) was judged to be at low risk of bias, twelve studies (12/15) raised some concerns,
and two studies (2/15) were at high risk of bias. Domain-level assessment indicated that deviations from
the intended interventions (D2) were the most common issue, raising some concerns in 14 out of 15 stud-
ies (14/15). Missing outcome data (D3) raised concerns in three studies (3/15), and selection of the reported
result (D5) raised concerns in two studies (2/15). In contrast, the randomisation process (D1) demonstrated
high methodological quality across most studies (14/15 at low risk), and measurement of the outcome (D4)
was at low risk in most studies (13/15). These limitations, largely related to deviations from intended inter-
ventions, may have attenuated the estimated intervention effects.


3.4. Evaluation of meta-analysis results
3.4.1. Overall effect test
A meta-analysis of 15 randomised and cluster-randomised trials (n = 7,465) showed that exercise-based
prevention programmes significantly reduced the risk of HSI in football participants (RR = 0.51, 95% CI
0.36–0.71; p < 0.0001), corresponding to an approximately 49% relative risk reduction (1 − RR).
Between-study heterogeneity was moderate (I2 = 57%, τ2 = 0.20). The 95% prediction interval ranged
from 0.18 to 1.40. It crossed the line of no effect (RR = 1), indicating that the magnitude of benefit might
vary across implementation contexts. 14 of the 15 studies had point estimates favouring the intervention
(RR < 1), supporting consistency in the direction of the overall effect (Figure 3).

3.4.2. Subgroup analyses stratified by training dose, adherence, and playing level
There was no evidence of interaction by dose-related parameters, including training frequency, session
duration, and weekly training volume (P for interaction = 0.54, 0.72, and 0.62, respectively; Supplementary
Figure S1). Effect estimates consistently favoured the intervention across dose strata. Effects were
broadly comparable for 1–2 sessions/week (k = 8; RR = 0.56, 95% CI 0.38–0.83) and 3–4 sessions/week
(k = 7; RR = 0.45, 95% CI 0.24–0.84). Similarly, both 1–30 min/week (k = 6; RR = 0.42, 95% CI 0.26–0.68)
and 30–60 min/week (k = 4; RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.27–0.96) were associated with a lower HSI risk.
    In contrast, there was evidence of subgroup differences by intervention duration, adherence, and
playing level (P for interaction = 0.04, <0.00001, and 0.02, respectively). Interventions lasting 1–6 months
(k = 9) were associated with a reduced HSI risk (RR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.28–0.66; p = 0.0001), whereas the
7- to 10-month subgroup (k = 6) did not reach statistical significance (RR = 0.77, 95% CI 0.54–1.09;
p = 0.14).
    Adherence showed the strongest evidence of effect modification. High adherence (≥75%; k = 10) was
associated with a substantial reduction in HSI risk (RR = 0.36, 95% CI 0.28–0.48; p < 0.00001), whereas low
adherence (<75%; k = 4) showed no clear benefit (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23; p = 0.56). According to
playing level, the association appeared stronger in elite/semi-professional players (k = 8; RR = 0.38, 95%
CI 0.23–0.61; p < 0.0001), whereas the amateur subgroup (k = 7) was not statistically significant (RR = 0.77,
95% CI 0.53–1.10; p = 0.15).
