414	3.4.3. Adherence-stratified analyses
415	Adherence consistently modified intervention effects across populations and contexts (Supplementary
416	Figure S2). Across strata, the pooled RR under low adherence (<75%) was close to 1 and non-significant:
417	adults (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23), amateur athletes (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23), male athletes
418	(RR = 0.94, 95% CI 0.72–1.22), and strength-based interventions (RR = 0.94, 95% CI 0.72–1.22). A
419	similar pattern was observed for eccentric-based interventions: under low adherence (<75%), the
420	pooled RR was 0.96 (95% CI 0.70–1.32), whereas under high adherence (≥75%), the pooled RR was
421	0.36, 95% CI 0.27–0.48. By contrast, high adherence (≥75%) was consistently associated with a sub-
422	stantial and statistically significant reduction in HSI risk across these strata (high-adherence pooled
423	RRs clustered around 0.34–0.38: adults RR = 0.34, 0.25–0.46; amateurs RR = 0.38, 0.28–0.52; males RR
424	= 0.35, 0.26–0.47; strength-based interventions RR = 0.36, 0.28–0.48; eccentric-based interventions RR
425	= 0.36, 95% CI 0.27–0.48). The between-adherence subgroup differences were statistically significant
426	within each stratum (P for interaction < 0.00001 throughout). Some strata might draw on overlap-
427	ping sets of trials, which could yield identical or near-identical pooled estimates across related
428	stratifications.
429	                                                                                             Annals of Medicine   9
430	
431	
432	
433	
434	Figure 3. Pooled effect of exercise-based prevention programmes on football participants.
435	
436	3.4.4. Exploratory subgroup analyses: intervention type, programme components, and complexity
437	Exploratory subgroup analyses examined whether intervention type and selected programme compo-
438	nents (or programme complexity) were associated with differential effects on HSI risk. Point estimates
439	generally favoured the intervention across strata. However, there was no evidence of subgroup differ-
440	ences for any comparison (all P for interaction > 0.05; Supplementary Figure S3). Given the exploratory
441	nature of these analyses and the limited number of trials within several strata (as few as k = 3 in some
442	comparisons, although the eccentric training stratum included k = 12), these findings should not be inter-
443	preted as evidence of equivalence between programmes.
444	   By intervention type, FIFA 11+ (RR = 0.53, 95% CI 0.29–0.97; k = 4) and NHE-based programmes (RR =
445	0.46, 0.26–0.84; k = 7) were each associated with significant risk reductions, whereas other interventions
446	were not (RR = 0.53, 0.24–1.18; k = 4); effects did not differ between intervention types (P for interaction
447	= 0.94).
448	   In addition, component-based analyses showed no evidence of subgroup differences by inclusion of
449	balance training (p = 0.37), plyometrics (p = 0.22), agility/speed training (p = 0.69), flexibility training
450	(p = 0.97), or programme complexity (single/dual vs multicomponent; p = 0.69). For eccentric training, the
451	stratum including eccentric exercise showed a significant protective association (RR = 0.48, 0.33–0.70;
452	k = 12), whereas the stratum without eccentric training did not (RR = 0.74, 0.36–1.53; k = 3). Nevertheless,
453	the between-stratum difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.28).
454	
455	
456	3.4.5. Meta-regression: adherence as a predictor of intervention effects
457	One study did not report adherence; therefore, the meta-regression included 14 trials (k = 14).
458	Random-effects meta-regression showed a significant inverse linear association between adherence (%)
459	and intervention effects on the logRR scale (β = −0.0190, 95% CI −0.0272 to −0.0109; p < 0.001). This
460	corresponded to an RR multiplier = 0.83 (95% CI 0.76–0.90) for each 10-percentage-point increase in
461	adherence, equivalent to an approximate 17% reduction in RR (Supplementary Figure S4a). As this was
462	an aggregate-level analysis, causal inference requires caution.
463	   This dose–response association was consistent across prespecified subsets. Regression slopes were
464	similar (β ranging from −0.0178 to −0.0194; all p < 0.001), corresponding to RR multipliers of 0.82–0.84
465	 10      J. GU ET AL.
466	
467	
468	per 10-percentage-point increase in adherence: amateur athletes (k = 11; RR multiplier = 0.84, 95% CI
469	0.77–0.91), male athletes (k = 10; RR multiplier = 0.82, 95% CI 0.76–0.90), programmes including a strength
470	component (k = 13; RR multiplier = 0.83, 95% CI 0.76–0.90), and programmes including eccentric training
471	(k = 11; RR multiplier = 0.82, 95% CI 0.76–0.89; Supplementary Figure S4b–e). The close agreement across
472	subsets was consistent with a stable adherence–effect dose–response relationship.
473	
474	
475	3.5. Sensitivity analyses of the pooled effect
476	Leave-one-out analyses showed consistent protective effects after omitting any single study (pooled RR
477	range 0.33–0.64), with no single trial exerting undue influence on the overall estimate. A fixed-effect
478	model yielded similar results (RR = 0.55, 95% CI 0.46–0.66). Results were robust to the exclusion of stud-
479	ies judged to be at high risk of bias (RR = 0.54, 95% CI 0.38–0.76). Excluding the study that enrolled
480	referees did not materially change the pooled effect or heterogeneity (primary: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–
481	0.71; I2 = 57%; after exclusion: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.72; I2 = 59%) [36]. Omitting Engebretsen et al.
482	(2008) produced the largest reduction in heterogeneity (I2 = 48%) while maintaining a significant protec-
483	tive effect (RR = 0.46, 95% CI 0.33–0.64).
484	
485	
486	3.6. Assessment of publication bias
487	Formal tests provided no evidence of funnel plot asymmetry. Neither Egger’s regression test (p = 0.09) nor
488	Begg’s rank correlation test (p = 0.66) was statistically significant. Trim-and-fill analysis identified and
489	imputed three potentially missing studies; the adjusted pooled estimate was slightly attenuated but
490	remained in the protective direction (unadjusted: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.71; adjusted: RR = 0.54, 95%
491	CI 0.39–0.75), suggesting that any small study effect, if present, would have limited impact on the overall
492	conclusion (Figure 4). Overall, the available evidence does not suggest major publication bias, although
493	these tests might be underpowered with a modest number of trials, and minor asymmetry could not be
494	fully excluded.
495	
496	
497	3.7. GRADE assessment of the certainty of evidence
498	Certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. As all included studies were ran-
499	domised trials, initial certainty was high but was downgraded by two levels to low. One level was down-
500	graded for inconsistency due to moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%) and a prediction interval that crossed
501	the null, suggesting context-dependent effects. Another level was downgraded for risk of bias because
502	most trials raised some concerns or were at high risk of bias overall, predominantly driven by deviations
503	from intended interventions. No downgrading was applied for indirectness or imprecision because the
504	
505	
506	
507	
508	Figure 4. Funnel plot and trim-and-fill analysis assessing small study effects/publication bias for HSI.
509	                                                                                     Annals of Medicine     11
510	
511	
512	evidence directly addressed the review question, and the pooled confidence interval excluded the null.
513	Publication bias was not downgraded due to no clear evidence of asymmetry, acknowledging the limited
514	power of these assessments.
515	
516	
517	4. Discussion
518	4.1. Main findings
519	This systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 randomised controlled trials found that exercise-based
520	prevention programmes reduce the risk of HSI in football participants (RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.71,
521	p < 0.0001). By restricting inclusion to football-specific RCTs with HSI as the primary outcome, the present
522	synthesis provides estimates with enhanced specificity for applied football settings.
523	   The pooled effect exhibits moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%), and the 95% prediction interval crosses
524	the null (0.18–1.40), indicating that intervention effects may vary substantially across contexts. This vari-
525	ability suggests that real-world effectiveness is likely to differ depending on implementation conditions.
526	Implementation conditions may include how programmes are integrated into routine training, the level
527	of supervision and delivery fidelity, and the extent of sustained adherence and control-group contami-
528	nation. When adherence is included as a covariate in meta-regression, residual heterogeneity is markedly
529	attenuated (approaching zero), suggesting that variation in adherence may explain a substantial propor-
530	tion of between-study differences.
531	   The present study extends prior evidence by examining sources of heterogeneity rather than simply
532	estimating average efficacy. Specifically, we quantified the adherence–effect gradient using meta-regression
533	and examined prespecified effect modifiers (training dose, intervention duration, adherence, and playing
534	level), alongside exploratory comparisons of programme type, components, and complexity. Both pre-
535	specified subgroup analyses and meta-regression indicate that study-level adherence was consistently
536	associated with effect magnitude and demonstrate a dose–response pattern (β = −0.0190, p < 0.001). In
537	contrast, training dose and programme type show weaker or inconsistent associations with outcomes.
538	Accordingly, while exercise-based prevention programmes can reduce HSI risk in football, achieving
539	meaningful benefits in practice may be contingent on sustained adherence and favourable implementa-
540	tion conditions. Meanwhile, evidence is insufficient to reliably differentiate programme types or pre-
541	scribed training volumes within the ranges examined.
542	
543	
544	4.2. Training dose, adherence, and effect modifiers
545	The risk of bias assessment identifies deviations from intended interventions as the most common con-
546	cern, suggesting that implementation factors such as adherence, contamination, or dose delivery may
547	have attenuated between-group contrasts and contributed to heterogeneity. Similar implementation-related
548	limitations have been noted in prior hamstring injury prevention reviews [14].
549	
550	
551	4.2.1. Training dose
552	Subgroup analyses by training frequency, session duration, and weekly volume show no statistically sig-
553	nificant differences between dose strata, although point estimates generally favour protection across all
554	dose levels. Specifically, interventions involving 1–2 sessions per week and 3–4 sessions per week are
555	both associated with reduced HSI risk, with no clear advantage for higher-frequency (RR = 0.56 vs 0.45;
556	P for interaction = 0.54). Similarly, weekly volumes of 1–30 and 30–60 min show comparable protective
557	effects (RR = 0.42 vs 0.51; P for interaction = 0.62). A meta-analysis of lower limb injuries reported no
558	effect for once-weekly hamstring eccentric training but a significant reduction for twice-weekly ham-
559	string eccentric training (RR = 1.00 vs 0.60) [51], which may reflect differences in injury outcomes, par-
560	ticipant populations, and intervention implementation across reviews. In contrast, in this study’s
561	football-specific HSI synthesis, both 1–2 and 3–4 sessions/week are similarly protective with no evidence
562	of interaction, supporting the feasibility of lower-frequency prescriptions when adherence is maintained
563	[52]. These findings suggest that, within the dose ranges examined, both lower and higher prescribed
564	 12     J. GU ET AL.
565	
566	
567	doses may be effective provided they are implemented consistently. However, interpretation is limited by
568	inconsistent definitions of dose metrics across trials and by potential discrepancies between the pre-
569	scribed and completed dose, particularly in the context of low adherence. Consequently, given the lim-
570	ited statistical power due to small study numbers, the present data do not support strong inferences
571	regarding optimal dose thresholds.
572	
573	
574	4.2.2. Intervention duration and playing level
575	Shorter interventions (1–6 months) demonstrate statistically significant effects (RR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.28–
576	0.66), whereas longer interventions (7–10 months) do not reach statistical significance (RR = 0.77, 95% CI
577	0.54–1.09), with evidence of subgroup differences (p = 0.04). Similarly, elite and semi-professional popula-
578	tions show stronger effects (RR = 0.38, 95% CI 0.23–0.61) than amateur populations (RR = 0.77, 95% CI
579	0.53–1.10; P for interaction = 0.02). Because adherence emerged as a consistent effect modifier across
580	multiple analyses, these duration and level differences may partly reflect systematic variation in adher-
581	ence over time or across competitive contexts [17]. However, the specific mechanisms underlying these
582	patterns are not directly examined in the included trials, and small study numbers within strata limit
583	definitive interpretation.
584	
585	
586	4.2.3. Adherence
587	Adherence emerges as the most consistent effect modifier. High-adherence trials (≥75%) show substan-
588	tial risk reduction (RR = 0.36, 95% CI 0.28–0.48), whereas low-adherence trials (<75%) cross the line of
589	no effect (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23; P for interaction < 0.00001). Meta-regression indicates a dose–
590	response relationship between adherence and effect magnitude (β = −0.0190, p < 0.001), corresponding
591	to an RR multiplier of 0.83 per 10-percentage-point increase in adherence. Practically, these findings
592	suggest that meaningful HSI risk reduction is most likely when teams achieve and sustain high adher-
593	ence (≥75% of prescribed sessions), with progressively smaller risk ratios as adherence increases. This
594	pattern is consistent across prespecified subgroup analyses and across extended adherence-stratified
595	analyses in different populations and implementation contexts.
596	    Additionally, the findings align with broader evidence suggesting that injury prevention effectiveness
597	increases with adherence [18,26,53]. Alternative explanations cannot be excluded. For example, trials
598	achieving high adherence may also have differed in implementation fidelity, participant motivation, or
599	control-group contamination. These findings should be interpreted as signals of effect modification and
600	sources of heterogeneity rather than definitive causal evidence. Individual-level adherence-outcome data
601	will be required to establish causality.
602	
603	
604	4.2.4. Intervention type and components
605	Exploratory comparisons of intervention types and programme components show no consistent differ-
606	ences. Given limited statistical power, small study numbers, and variability in intervention reporting and
607	delivery, these findings should be interpreted as insufficient evidence to differentiate programme types
608	rather than evidence of equivalence. Future trials should improve specification and reporting of both
609	prescribed content and implementation processes, including adherence, fidelity, and progression, to
610	enable more informative comparisons [27].
611	
612	
613	4.3. Implications for practice
614	The present findings suggest three considerations for implementing exercise-based HSI prevention pro-
615	grammes in football.
616	    First, adherence appears to be an important determinant of intervention effectiveness. High-adherence
617	trials demonstrate clear risk reduction, whereas low-adherence trials show attenuated effects [45].
618	Accordingly, routinely monitoring adherence and providing regular feedback within teams is likely a key
619	implementation strategy to support sustained adherence and high-fidelity delivery. Programme selection
620	                                                                                     Annals of Medicine     13
621	
622	
623	and delivery should therefore account for feasibility and sustainability within the team environment
624	[18,53].
625	   Second, training frequency and weekly volume in the ranges examined (1–4 sessions per week;
626	1–60 min per week) are both associated with protective effects, with no clear advantage for higher pre-
627	scribed doses. This does not preclude differences by completed dose, which may deviate from the pre-
628	scribed dose under variable adherence. These findings suggest that programmes can be effective across
629	a range of dose levels, provided they are implemented consistently.
630	   Third, shorter intervention durations and elite/semi-professional populations show stronger effects
631	than longer interventions or amateur populations. Given that adherence is the most consistent effect
632	modifier across analyses, these differences may partly reflect variation in adherence over time or across
633	competitive levels [47].
634	
635	
636	4.4. Limitations
637	Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
638	    First, moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%) and a prediction interval crossing the null (0.18–1.40) suggest
639	that effects may vary across contexts, and the pooled estimate reflects an average effect.
640	    Second, dose and adherence are inconsistently defined and reported across trials, limiting compara-
641	bility. Several included trials used cluster randomisation, and it was not always clear whether clustering
642	was consistently accounted for in the original trial analyses; if clustering is not accounted for, precision
643	may be overstated. In addition, adherence was extracted from trial reports and may vary in definition
644	and measurement accuracy across studies, which could bias the estimated adherence–effect relationship.
645	Subgroup and meta-regression analyses are conducted at the study level and are susceptible to ecolog-
646	ical bias and confounding; adherence-outcome associations do not establish individual-level causality,
647	and alternative explanations (such as differences in implementation fidelity or participant motivation)
648	cannot be excluded. These analyses are therefore hypothesis-generating rather than causal. Third, sub-
649	group analyses are based on small numbers of studies, and multiple comparisons increase the risk of
650	chance findings; these exploratory results require confirmation.
651	    Finally, generalizability is limited because most trials enrolled male players (11/15 male-only), and the
652	small number of female-only trials (4/15) precluded sex-stratified analyses; extrapolation to female foot-
653	ball, youth populations, and other team sports should, therefore, be cautious.
654	
655	
656	4.5. Future research
657	Several priorities for future research emerge from these findings. First, future trials should standardise
658	reporting of training exposure and adherence using consistent definitions and core metrics, including
659	session frequency, duration, progression, and attendance; basic process measures such as execution qual-
660	ity should also be documented to improve interpretability and enable cross-study comparisons. Second,
661	comparative evaluations using head-to-head or factorial designs, with cluster randomisation where
662	appropriate, will help clarify which programme components or combinations are associated with benefit,
663	alongside monitoring of control-group activities to mitigate contamination. Third, adequately powered
664	studies in female football and youth populations, together with pragmatic club-based implementation
665	research, are needed to strengthen external validity and inform scalable delivery strategies.
666	
667	
668	5. Conclusions
669	Exercise-based hamstring injury prevention programmes reduce the risk of HSI in football participants.
670	Adherence is consistently associated with effect magnitude across multiple stratifications, with preventive
671	benefit concentrated in high-adherence implementations. Subgroup patterns also suggest differences by
672	intervention duration and playing level. Within the examined prescribed-dose ranges, there was no clear
673	additional advantage of higher-frequency versus lower-frequency prescriptions, nor of higher weekly
674	training time versus lower weekly training time. Evidence remains insufficient to reliably rank programme
675	 14     J. GU ET AL.
676	
677	
678	types or specific component configurations. Accordingly, programme selection should prioritise feasibil-
679	ity, and delivery should prioritise maintaining high adherence and implementation fidelity to maximise
680	reproducible preventive gains.
681	
682	
683	Acknowledgements
684	The authors would like to express their sincere gratitude to all researchers whose work contributed to this review
685	and meta-analysis.
686	
687	
688	Ethical approval information

3.4.3. Adherence-stratified analyses
Adherence consistently modified intervention effects across populations and contexts (Supplementary
Figure S2). Across strata, the pooled RR under low adherence (<75%) was close to 1 and non-significant:
adults (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23), amateur athletes (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23), male athletes
(RR = 0.94, 95% CI 0.72–1.22), and strength-based interventions (RR = 0.94, 95% CI 0.72–1.22). A
similar pattern was observed for eccentric-based interventions: under low adherence (<75%), the
pooled RR was 0.96 (95% CI 0.70–1.32), whereas under high adherence (≥75%), the pooled RR was
0.36, 95% CI 0.27–0.48. By contrast, high adherence (≥75%) was consistently associated with a sub-
stantial and statistically significant reduction in HSI risk across these strata (high-adherence pooled
RRs clustered around 0.34–0.38: adults RR = 0.34, 0.25–0.46; amateurs RR = 0.38, 0.28–0.52; males RR
= 0.35, 0.26–0.47; strength-based interventions RR = 0.36, 0.28–0.48; eccentric-based interventions RR
= 0.36, 95% CI 0.27–0.48). The between-adherence subgroup differences were statistically significant
within each stratum (P for interaction < 0.00001 throughout). Some strata might draw on overlap-
ping sets of trials, which could yield identical or near-identical pooled estimates across related
stratifications.

3.4.4. Exploratory subgroup analyses: intervention type, programme components, and complexity
Exploratory subgroup analyses examined whether intervention type and selected programme compo-
nents (or programme complexity) were associated with differential effects on HSI risk. Point estimates
generally favoured the intervention across strata. However, there was no evidence of subgroup differ-
ences for any comparison (all P for interaction > 0.05; Supplementary Figure S3). Given the exploratory
nature of these analyses and the limited number of trials within several strata (as few as k = 3 in some
comparisons, although the eccentric training stratum included k = 12), these findings should not be inter-
preted as evidence of equivalence between programmes.
   By intervention type, FIFA 11+ (RR = 0.53, 95% CI 0.29–0.97; k = 4) and NHE-based programmes (RR =
0.46, 0.26–0.84; k = 7) were each associated with significant risk reductions, whereas other interventions
were not (RR = 0.53, 0.24–1.18; k = 4); effects did not differ between intervention types (P for interaction
= 0.94).
   In addition, component-based analyses showed no evidence of subgroup differences by inclusion of
balance training (p = 0.37), plyometrics (p = 0.22), agility/speed training (p = 0.69), flexibility training
(p = 0.97), or programme complexity (single/dual vs multicomponent; p = 0.69). For eccentric training, the
stratum including eccentric exercise showed a significant protective association (RR = 0.48, 0.33–0.70;
k = 12), whereas the stratum without eccentric training did not (RR = 0.74, 0.36–1.53; k = 3). Nevertheless,
the between-stratum difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.28).


3.4.5. Meta-regression: adherence as a predictor of intervention effects
One study did not report adherence; therefore, the meta-regression included 14 trials (k = 14).
Random-effects meta-regression showed a significant inverse linear association between adherence (%)
and intervention effects on the logRR scale (β = −0.0190, 95% CI −0.0272 to −0.0109; p < 0.001). This
corresponded to an RR multiplier = 0.83 (95% CI 0.76–0.90) for each 10-percentage-point increase in
adherence, equivalent to an approximate 17% reduction in RR (Supplementary Figure S4a). As this was
an aggregate-level analysis, causal inference requires caution.
   This dose–response association was consistent across prespecified subsets. Regression slopes were
similar (β ranging from −0.0178 to −0.0194; all p < 0.001), corresponding to RR multipliers of 0.82–0.84
 10      J. GU ET AL.


per 10-percentage-point increase in adherence: amateur athletes (k = 11; RR multiplier = 0.84, 95% CI
0.77–0.91), male athletes (k = 10; RR multiplier = 0.82, 95% CI 0.76–0.90), programmes including a strength
component (k = 13; RR multiplier = 0.83, 95% CI 0.76–0.90), and programmes including eccentric training
(k = 11; RR multiplier = 0.82, 95% CI 0.76–0.89; Supplementary Figure S4b–e). The close agreement across
subsets was consistent with a stable adherence–effect dose–response relationship.


3.5. Sensitivity analyses of the pooled effect
Leave-one-out analyses showed consistent protective effects after omitting any single study (pooled RR
range 0.33–0.64), with no single trial exerting undue influence on the overall estimate. A fixed-effect
model yielded similar results (RR = 0.55, 95% CI 0.46–0.66). Results were robust to the exclusion of stud-
ies judged to be at high risk of bias (RR = 0.54, 95% CI 0.38–0.76). Excluding the study that enrolled
referees did not materially change the pooled effect or heterogeneity (primary: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–
0.71; I2 = 57%; after exclusion: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.72; I2 = 59%) [36]. Omitting Engebretsen et al.
(2008) produced the largest reduction in heterogeneity (I2 = 48%) while maintaining a significant protec-
tive effect (RR = 0.46, 95% CI 0.33–0.64).


3.6. Assessment of publication bias
Formal tests provided no evidence of funnel plot asymmetry. Neither Egger’s regression test (p = 0.09) nor
Begg’s rank correlation test (p = 0.66) was statistically significant. Trim-and-fill analysis identified and
imputed three potentially missing studies; the adjusted pooled estimate was slightly attenuated but
remained in the protective direction (unadjusted: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.71; adjusted: RR = 0.54, 95%
CI 0.39–0.75), suggesting that any small study effect, if present, would have limited impact on the overall
conclusion (Figure 4). Overall, the available evidence does not suggest major publication bias, although
these tests might be underpowered with a modest number of trials, and minor asymmetry could not be
fully excluded.


3.7. GRADE assessment of the certainty of evidence
Certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. As all included studies were ran-
domised trials, initial certainty was high but was downgraded by two levels to low. One level was down-
graded for inconsistency due to moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%) and a prediction interval that crossed
the null, suggesting context-dependent effects. Another level was downgraded for risk of bias because
most trials raised some concerns or were at high risk of bias overall, predominantly driven by deviations
from intended interventions. No downgrading was applied for indirectness or imprecision because the

evidence directly addressed the review question, and the pooled confidence interval excluded the null.
Publication bias was not downgraded due to no clear evidence of asymmetry, acknowledging the limited
power of these assessments.


4. Discussion
4.1. Main findings
This systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 randomised controlled trials found that exercise-based
prevention programmes reduce the risk of HSI in football participants (RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.71,
p < 0.0001). By restricting inclusion to football-specific RCTs with HSI as the primary outcome, the present
synthesis provides estimates with enhanced specificity for applied football settings.
   The pooled effect exhibits moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%), and the 95% prediction interval crosses
the null (0.18–1.40), indicating that intervention effects may vary substantially across contexts. This vari-
ability suggests that real-world effectiveness is likely to differ depending on implementation conditions.
Implementation conditions may include how programmes are integrated into routine training, the level
of supervision and delivery fidelity, and the extent of sustained adherence and control-group contami-
nation. When adherence is included as a covariate in meta-regression, residual heterogeneity is markedly
attenuated (approaching zero), suggesting that variation in adherence may explain a substantial propor-
tion of between-study differences.
   The present study extends prior evidence by examining sources of heterogeneity rather than simply
estimating average efficacy. Specifically, we quantified the adherence–effect gradient using meta-regression
and examined prespecified effect modifiers (training dose, intervention duration, adherence, and playing
level), alongside exploratory comparisons of programme type, components, and complexity. Both pre-
specified subgroup analyses and meta-regression indicate that study-level adherence was consistently
associated with effect magnitude and demonstrate a dose–response pattern (β = −0.0190, p < 0.001). In
contrast, training dose and programme type show weaker or inconsistent associations with outcomes.
Accordingly, while exercise-based prevention programmes can reduce HSI risk in football, achieving
meaningful benefits in practice may be contingent on sustained adherence and favourable implementa-
tion conditions. Meanwhile, evidence is insufficient to reliably differentiate programme types or pre-
scribed training volumes within the ranges examined.


4.2. Training dose, adherence, and effect modifiers
The risk of bias assessment identifies deviations from intended interventions as the most common con-
cern, suggesting that implementation factors such as adherence, contamination, or dose delivery may
have attenuated between-group contrasts and contributed to heterogeneity. Similar implementation-related
limitations have been noted in prior hamstring injury prevention reviews [14].


4.2.1. Training dose
Subgroup analyses by training frequency, session duration, and weekly volume show no statistically sig-
nificant differences between dose strata, although point estimates generally favour protection across all
dose levels. Specifically, interventions involving 1–2 sessions per week and 3–4 sessions per week are
both associated with reduced HSI risk, with no clear advantage for higher-frequency (RR = 0.56 vs 0.45;
P for interaction = 0.54). Similarly, weekly volumes of 1–30 and 30–60 min show comparable protective
effects (RR = 0.42 vs 0.51; P for interaction = 0.62). A meta-analysis of lower limb injuries reported no
effect for once-weekly hamstring eccentric training but a significant reduction for twice-weekly ham-
string eccentric training (RR = 1.00 vs 0.60) [51], which may reflect differences in injury outcomes, par-
ticipant populations, and intervention implementation across reviews. In contrast, in this study’s
football-specific HSI synthesis, both 1–2 and 3–4 sessions/week are similarly protective with no evidence
of interaction, supporting the feasibility of lower-frequency prescriptions when adherence is maintained
[52]. These findings suggest that, within the dose ranges examined, both lower and higher prescribed
 12     J. GU ET AL.


doses may be effective provided they are implemented consistently. However, interpretation is limited by
inconsistent definitions of dose metrics across trials and by potential discrepancies between the pre-
scribed and completed dose, particularly in the context of low adherence. Consequently, given the lim-
ited statistical power due to small study numbers, the present data do not support strong inferences
regarding optimal dose thresholds.


4.2.2. Intervention duration and playing level
Shorter interventions (1–6 months) demonstrate statistically significant effects (RR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.28–
0.66), whereas longer interventions (7–10 months) do not reach statistical significance (RR = 0.77, 95% CI
0.54–1.09), with evidence of subgroup differences (p = 0.04). Similarly, elite and semi-professional popula-
tions show stronger effects (RR = 0.38, 95% CI 0.23–0.61) than amateur populations (RR = 0.77, 95% CI
0.53–1.10; P for interaction = 0.02). Because adherence emerged as a consistent effect modifier across
multiple analyses, these duration and level differences may partly reflect systematic variation in adher-
ence over time or across competitive contexts [17]. However, the specific mechanisms underlying these
patterns are not directly examined in the included trials, and small study numbers within strata limit
definitive interpretation.


4.2.3. Adherence
Adherence emerges as the most consistent effect modifier. High-adherence trials (≥75%) show substan-
tial risk reduction (RR = 0.36, 95% CI 0.28–0.48), whereas low-adherence trials (<75%) cross the line of
no effect (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23; P for interaction < 0.00001). Meta-regression indicates a dose–
response relationship between adherence and effect magnitude (β = −0.0190, p < 0.001), corresponding
to an RR multiplier of 0.83 per 10-percentage-point increase in adherence. Practically, these findings
suggest that meaningful HSI risk reduction is most likely when teams achieve and sustain high adher-
ence (≥75% of prescribed sessions), with progressively smaller risk ratios as adherence increases. This
pattern is consistent across prespecified subgroup analyses and across extended adherence-stratified
analyses in different populations and implementation contexts.
    Additionally, the findings align with broader evidence suggesting that injury prevention effectiveness
increases with adherence [18,26,53]. Alternative explanations cannot be excluded. For example, trials
achieving high adherence may also have differed in implementation fidelity, participant motivation, or
control-group contamination. These findings should be interpreted as signals of effect modification and
sources of heterogeneity rather than definitive causal evidence. Individual-level adherence-outcome data
will be required to establish causality.


4.2.4. Intervention type and components
Exploratory comparisons of intervention types and programme components show no consistent differ-
ences. Given limited statistical power, small study numbers, and variability in intervention reporting and
delivery, these findings should be interpreted as insufficient evidence to differentiate programme types
rather than evidence of equivalence. Future trials should improve specification and reporting of both
prescribed content and implementation processes, including adherence, fidelity, and progression, to
enable more informative comparisons [27].


4.3. Implications for practice
The present findings suggest three considerations for implementing exercise-based HSI prevention pro-
grammes in football.
    First, adherence appears to be an important determinant of intervention effectiveness. High-adherence
trials demonstrate clear risk reduction, whereas low-adherence trials show attenuated effects [45].
Accordingly, routinely monitoring adherence and providing regular feedback within teams is likely a key
implementation strategy to support sustained adherence and high-fidelity delivery. Programme selection
                                                                                     Annals of Medicine     13


and delivery should therefore account for feasibility and sustainability within the team environment
[18,53].
   Second, training frequency and weekly volume in the ranges examined (1–4 sessions per week;
1–60 min per week) are both associated with protective effects, with no clear advantage for higher pre-
scribed doses. This does not preclude differences by completed dose, which may deviate from the pre-
scribed dose under variable adherence. These findings suggest that programmes can be effective across
a range of dose levels, provided they are implemented consistently.
   Third, shorter intervention durations and elite/semi-professional populations show stronger effects
than longer interventions or amateur populations. Given that adherence is the most consistent effect
modifier across analyses, these differences may partly reflect variation in adherence over time or across
competitive levels [47].


4.4. Limitations
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
    First, moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%) and a prediction interval crossing the null (0.18–1.40) suggest
that effects may vary across contexts, and the pooled estimate reflects an average effect.
    Second, dose and adherence are inconsistently defined and reported across trials, limiting compara-
bility. Several included trials used cluster randomisation, and it was not always clear whether clustering
was consistently accounted for in the original trial analyses; if clustering is not accounted for, precision
may be overstated. In addition, adherence was extracted from trial reports and may vary in definition
and measurement accuracy across studies, which could bias the estimated adherence–effect relationship.
Subgroup and meta-regression analyses are conducted at the study level and are susceptible to ecolog-
ical bias and confounding; adherence-outcome associations do not establish individual-level causality,
and alternative explanations (such as differences in implementation fidelity or participant motivation)
cannot be excluded. These analyses are therefore hypothesis-generating rather than causal. Third, sub-
group analyses are based on small numbers of studies, and multiple comparisons increase the risk of
chance findings; these exploratory results require confirmation.
    Finally, generalizability is limited because most trials enrolled male players (11/15 male-only), and the
small number of female-only trials (4/15) precluded sex-stratified analyses; extrapolation to female foot-
ball, youth populations, and other team sports should, therefore, be cautious.


4.5. Future research
Several priorities for future research emerge from these findings. First, future trials should standardise
reporting of training exposure and adherence using consistent definitions and core metrics, including
session frequency, duration, progression, and attendance; basic process measures such as execution qual-
ity should also be documented to improve interpretability and enable cross-study comparisons. Second,
comparative evaluations using head-to-head or factorial designs, with cluster randomisation where
appropriate, will help clarify which programme components or combinations are associated with benefit,
alongside monitoring of control-group activities to mitigate contamination. Third, adequately powered
studies in female football and youth populations, together with pragmatic club-based implementation
research, are needed to strengthen external validity and inform scalable delivery strategies.


5. Conclusions
Exercise-based hamstring injury prevention programmes reduce the risk of HSI in football participants.
Adherence is consistently associated with effect magnitude across multiple stratifications, with preventive
benefit concentrated in high-adherence implementations. Subgroup patterns also suggest differences by
intervention duration and playing level. Within the examined prescribed-dose ranges, there was no clear
additional advantage of higher-frequency versus lower-frequency prescriptions, nor of higher weekly
training time versus lower weekly training time. Evidence remains insufficient to reliably rank programme
 14     J. GU ET AL.


types or specific component configurations. Accordingly, programme selection should prioritise feasibil-
ity, and delivery should prioritise maintaining high adherence and implementation fidelity to maximise
reproducible preventive gains.

{
 "id": "Q04",
 "sourceFile": "Intervention components, training dose, and adherence in exercise-based prevention of hamstring strain injury in football - a systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text matches the filename ('Intervention components, training dose, and adherence in exercise-based prevention of hamstring strain injury in football: a systematic review and meta-analysis') and the printed article DOI is 10.1080/07853890.2026.2652116.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Performance", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Collegiate", "Youth / Adolescent", "Adult / Recreational", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 15 randomised and cluster-randomised trials (n = 7,465) of exercise-based hamstring injury prevention in football participants, compared with usual practice or standard warm-up. Programmes reduced hamstring strain risk (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.71; I2 57%), with a prediction interval crossing the null (0.18 to 1.40). The authors report the benefit was concentrated in high-adherence implementations (RR 0.36 at 75% or more adherence vs RR 0.92 below 75%), and rate the certainty of evidence as low.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Adherence and dose were defined inconsistently across trials, and the adherence finding comes from study-level meta-regression across 14 trials, which cannot establish individual-level causality. Eleven of the 15 trials enrolled only male players, so the female and youth evidence is small.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the adherence and dose findings as a proven programme design rule, but the authors describe them as hypothesis-generating and say the evidence cannot rank programme types or components.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2026,
   "citation": "Gu J, Li Y, Wang Y, Zhang Y. Intervention components, training dose, and adherence in exercise-based prevention of hamstring strain injury in football: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Ann Med. 2026;58(1):2652116.",
   "doi": "10.1080/07853890.2026.2652116",
   "abstract": "This meta-analysis pooled 15 randomised and cluster-randomised trials (n = 7,465) of exercise-based hamstring injury prevention in football. Programmes reduced hamstring strain risk, and the effect was largest when players completed at least 75% of prescribed sessions. Programme type and components could not be reliably separated.",
   "tldr": "Exercise-based hamstring prevention roughly halved hamstring strain risk across 15 football trials, but the benefit appeared only when players completed most of the prescribed sessions. The review cannot say which programme type or component works best.",
   "methods": "Six databases were searched to 1 October 2025 (PROSPERO CRD420251246295) for randomised and cluster-randomised trials comparing an exercise-based hamstring prevention programme with usual practice or a standard warm-up in football participants. Random-effects meta-analysis pooled risk ratios, with prespecified subgroup analyses and meta-regression for training dose, adherence and playing level, and quality was judged with RoB 2 and GRADE.",
   "findings": "The overall RR was 0.51 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.71), equal to 38 fewer hamstring injuries per 1000 participants on a control event rate of 7.8% (95% CI 23 to 50 fewer). High adherence (at least 75%) gave RR 0.36 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.48), against RR 0.92 (95% CI 0.68 to 1.23) for low adherence (P for interaction below 0.00001). Meta-regression across 14 trials gave an RR multiplier of 0.83 per 10 percentage points of adherence, while training frequency and weekly volume did not change the effect.",
   "limitations": "Heterogeneity was moderate (I2 57%) with a prediction interval crossing the null, and the subgroup and meta-regression results are study-level and exploratory. The Discussion states that residual heterogeneity falls close to zero after adding adherence, but no residual I2 or tau2 is reported in the Results, so that claim cannot be checked. Trim-and-fill gave an adjusted RR of 0.54 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.75), and the certainty of evidence was rated low.",
   "practicalImplications": "Track session completion for each player, because the benefit was seen only at high adherence (at least 75% of prescribed sessions). Within the 1 to 4 sessions per week and 1 to 60 minutes per week range studied, higher frequency or volume gave no clear extra benefit, so lower-frequency plans can work if they are delivered consistently. The review does not show that one programme type or exercise component is superior to another.",
   "athleteDev": "For performance staff, the practical point is that protection depended on players completing the programme, so completion should be tracked alongside the prescription.
